objects.label: Astronomia hypothetica quadriformis (Frobenius autograph)
objects.notes: RE-ATTRIBUTED 2026-05-31: the KB creator field names Georg Ludwig Frobenius (1566–1645), and the title compares Tycho's system WITH Longomontanus's (drawing on the Astronomia Danica, 1622) — so this is Frobenius's own 17th-c. autograph treatise, NOT a Tycho manuscript. Tycho appears only as one of the four world-systems. A Nachleben/reception object, not a Tycho autograph. PROVENANCE (2026-06-01, LOW conf.): Frobenius was a Hamburg printer-bookseller who spent ~6 weeks in Tycho's familia on Hven in 1591 and printed Longomontanus's Cyclometria (Hamburg 1627) — not of the Basel Froben dynasty though he thought so (Christianson, On Tycho's Island pp.285–86). Route into KB unconfirmed: likeliest the Gottorp Castle library (Holstein material, transferred to Copenhagen 1713–49) or a direct Danish-court channel; GKS shelfmark = entry before 1785. No print/sibling copy found (absent VD17/USTC/WorldCat) — apparently unique. CFC 2026-06-01: KB record confirms creator 'Georgius Ludovicus Frobenius 1566–1645 matematiker boghandler', GKS 320 folio, date '16??', 1 vol., Latin; only catalogue datum is 'Indlemmet i KB senest 1787'. PROVENANCE now documented from Brøndsted 1962 (p.77 + n.10): GKS 320 is one of a 3-vol. set of Frobenius printer's-manuscripts (Druckmanuskripte for publications he never issued) — GKS 320–322 2° = this 'Astronomia hypothetica quadriformis' + an 'Astrologia Ovidiana'. On Frobenius's death (Hamburg 1645) his literary remains passed to the Hamburg cathedral chapter (Domkapitel/Dombibliothek); when the Dombibliothek was dissolved and auctioned in the 18th c., KB Copenhagen acquired them 'perhaps for their use of Tycho-Brahe material' — squaring with 'Indlemmet senest 1787'. Channel = Frobenius → Hamburg Dombibliothek → 18th-c. auction → KB (NOT Gottorp). Not digitised. The same Brøndsted article published a new Tycho poem from a Frobenius proof-sheet (O_STOCKHOLM_FROBENIUS_CARMEN). Frobenius's autobiog. MS = NKS 2596 fol.

Long exhibited as 'annotated by Tycho', but Gingerich & Westman 1981 proved the marginalia are Paul Wittich's hand (c.1546–1586), not Tycho's; corroborated by Rosen 1981 and Šíma–Valeška 2002. Tycho was the OWNER: he acquired Wittich's books — incl. this copy — from Wittich's sister via Jakob Monau, after Wittich's death. Documentary anchor: Monau's signed attestation (Prague, 23 Oct 1600) that the related comet leaves in KB GKS 1826 are Wittich's hand. Jesuit inscription (1642) confirms Tychonic provenance. THE canonical Wittich-not-Tycho misattribution — see the Debunked Claims Register and the Graphonomicon paul-wittich discriminator.

objects.label: Triangulorum planorum [et sphæricorum] praxis arithmetica (1591)
objects.notes: SHELFMARK CONFIRMED 2026-06-01: Prague, National Library of the Czech Republic (formerly the University Library), NK 14 C 20 (old marks Truhlář nr 2761 / Kl. nr 12:2). Tycho's trigonometry, dated 1591, in its original binding as the closing item of a Sammelband opened by Rheticus's Canon doctrinae triangulorum (Norlind 1970 p.234; 'Tycho Brahe and Prague — Crossroads of European Science'). Two editions exist: Studnička's 1886 Prague phototype facsimile and Dreyer's critical text TBOO I, 283–293 (made from this MS). HAND (settled): the content is Tycho's, the script is not his autograph. Dreyer (TBOO I, 315) doubted Studnička's autograph attribution, and Šíma & Valeška 2002 (Tycho Brahe and Prague, pp.150–167) prove NK 14 C 20 is by a professional calligrapher — 'Not one of the manuscripts held by the National Library, Prague was written by Tycho's hand'. Studnička's 1901 autograph claim is in the Debunked Claims Register.

objects.label: Tycho's elegy on Ptolemy (1584) — in Frobenius's 1644 proof-sheet
objects.notes: A hitherto-unknown Latin elegy by Tycho in praise of Claudius Ptolemy, headed 'In effigiem Cl. Ptolemæi Alexandrini. Elegia Tychonis Brahe, scripta A.C. 1584. Kal. VIIIbr.' — dated 1 Oct 1584, composed as an inscription to sit beneath a portrait of Ptolemy. 16 elegiac distichs (32 lines); incipit 'Hic oculos, faciem, barbam, sic membra gerebat / Claudius, is nomen cui Ptolemaeus erat.' — it sets Ptolemy's bloodless intellectual conquest of earth and heavens against Rome's bloody, partial conquest. Survives only on the LAST page of Georg Ludwig Frobenius's folio proof-sheet (prøveark) for his planned new Latin Almagest ('Claudii Ptolemæi Magnae Constructionis Mathematica … interpretatione Latine Georgii Ludov. Frobenii … ad … Christianum IV. Hamburgi, ex bibliopolio Frobeniano 1644'), identified at Kungliga biblioteket, Stockholm (KB Copenhagen holds a microfilm; Brøndsted gives no precise Stockholm shelfmark). Stockholm survival probably via Jørgen Seefeld's library → Swedish war-loot 1645. The poem predates Frobenius's 1591 Hven visit by 7 years; Brøndsted links it to the lost Latin minde-/tilegnelsesdigte Tycho wrote in autumn–winter 1584–85 to advertise his new Uraniborg press (cf. Q_LOST_POEMS) — Frobenius's print is an eftertryk detached from its original portrait. NOT in Dreyer's Opera Omnia: a genuine addition to the Tycho corpus. Published in full (facsimile p.73) by Mogens Brøndsted, 'Et ukendt digt af Tycho Brahe', Fund og Forskning 9 (1962) 71–78.

questions.title: Where are the 1593 observations? The 1593 fair-copy volume is missing.
questions.hypothesis: The Vienna apographa run jumps straight from 1592 (Cod. 10667) to 1594 (Cod. 10668) — no 1593 volume — confirming Dreyer (Opera Omnia X) that the 1593 fair-copy had disappeared before the series reached Vienna.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-30): The 1593 observations survive on the KB side. Codex K = GKS 1828 Fasc. I carries the substantial transcript of 1593 (ending with Venus, 25 Sep); the remainder sits on four leaves appended to the end of Codex E = GKS 313. Because only the Vienna copy was lost, the Historia Coelestis (printed from Vienna) almost wholly omits 1593 — exactly the loss Bartholin's separate transcript repaired. Cf. Carman & Recio (2022) on the surviving 1593 Appendix. The 1593 fair-copy volume itself is genuinely lost, not mis-shelved (Cod. 10673 = 1599, not a stray 1593).

questions.title: Collate the Vienna apographa against the KB autograph protocols, year by year
questions.hypothesis: KB holds the originals (nightly logs, grouped in multi-year folio/quarto volumes); Vienna holds the neat yearly recopies 1582–1601. The two halves had never been laid out against each other in a single year-by-year apparatus.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-30): The year-by-year KB-original ↔ Vienna-apographum mapping now exists — built from Dreyer's Opera Omnia X codex descriptions (Codices A–V) and the ÖNB Tabulae codicum VI (1873) leaf-count series, cross-checked against this project's own leaf counts. Each of the 19 apographa (Cod. 10657–10675) is now cross-linked to the KB autograph protocol(s) it fair-copies, with the Dreyer Codex letter and the documented gap for each year, together with a register of the known discrepancies and the precedent of Bartholin's 1668 Specimen. Two corrections fell out of the work: Cod. 10673 = 1599 (was mislabelled 'composite 1582–1601'), and GKS 312 spans 1587–1594 (fixed stars), not 1587–1590. The residual — reading-level spot-collation of individual copyist errors beyond Bartholin's 1582 Specimen — is carried forward as Q_SPOTCOLLATE.

questions.title: Reading-level spot-collation of apographum vs original for years beyond 1582
questions.hypothesis: The year-by-year structural mapping is settled (Q_APOGRAPHA_COLLATE). What remains is the fine collation — reading by reading — to catch individual copyist slips and silently dropped observations. Bartholin did this for 1582 in his Specimen recognitionis (1668, 36 pp.); Dreyer's printed Opera Omnia X–XIII embeds the rest by always following the KB original and flagging 'From Cod. V' where it filled a gap, but no free-standing variant register exists.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): a free-standing variant register now exists, built by mining the collation apparatus of Dreyer's Opera Omnia, where every divergence between the Vienna fair-copy and the KB original is a footnote keyed 'in cod. V'. Each recovered note is recorded with its TBOO page citation, binned by year and by type: a numeric copyist change (Codex D 28 → Cod. V 32, TBOO XI p.278), two Tycho additions present only in V (TBOO X pp.452, 472), a blank with a marginal doubt (TBOO III p.427), a deletion (TBOO III p.426), and an agreement control (p.423) — spanning the full typology. The ceiling is the print itself: the 1910s–20s volumes set the apparatus in small type that resists automated transcription, so only the cleanly-printed footnotes have been captured; extending the register toward exhaustiveness is mechanical, and waits on a fresh machine transcription of TBOO X–XIII or on manual page-reading at the discrepancy hot spots (1584, 1589–91, 1593).

questions.title: Reconcile the GKS 1829 content label (Codex L = 1585?) with Dreyer
questions.hypothesis: Dreyer Opera Omnia X describes Codex L = A. Coll. Reg. 1829 (4°, 214 ll.) as the transcript of the 1585 observations; the thesaurus record for GKS 1829 instead read 'computations, 1599–1600', which looked like a seed row-misalignment.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-30): NOT a seed error. The live KB catalogue (soeg.kb.dk; Ilsøe, Støbeskeen 1999 p.582) gives GKS 1829 the title 'Fasciculus Observationum Solis et Planetarum, subjuncto calculo Planetarum ex observationibus annorum 1599 et 1600' — i.e. 1599–1600, matching the seed. So the conflict is between Dreyer (1923) and the modern KB catalogue on the SAME shelfmark, not a data-entry slip. Neighbours GKS 1827/1828/1830 align Dreyer↔KB with no offset (ruling out a simple renumbering), and KB shelves no 214-leaf 1585 transcript under an obvious GKS number — a post-Dreyer rebinding of these 'modern-binding' quartos is the likeliest cause. GKS 1829 is now recorded per the live catalogue, with the Dreyer conflict noted on the object. The genuine residual — where Dreyer's 1585 Codex L lives today — is spun out as Q_1585_CODEXL.

questions.title: Locate the modern KB shelfmark of Dreyer's 1585 transcript (Codex L, 214 ll.)
questions.hypothesis: Dreyer's Codex L — a 214-leaf 4° transcript of the 1585 observations copied from the Vienna fair-copy, supplying readings the autograph Codex C (GKS 311) omits — is shelfmarked A. Coll. Reg. 1829 in Opera Omnia X, but GKS 1829 today is catalogued as a 1599–1600 fasciculus (Q_GKS1829).
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31, to the limit of catalogue evidence): an exhaustive KB Primo sweep (24 Brahe records) finds NO separately-catalogued 1585 observation transcript under any modern shelfmark — the only 1585 material is the distinct Codex M (GKS 1830). So Codex L was not renumbered to some other volume; GKS 1829 is its sole possible home. Crucially, the KB title for GKS 1829 ('Observationum Solis et Planetarum, subjuncto calculo Planetarum ex observationibus annorum 1599 et 1600') dates only the APPENDED calculation, not the main observations — fully compatible with Dreyer's Codex L (1585 observations + an appended planetary calculation he read as 1598). Best conclusion: GKS 1829 IS Dreyer's Codex L, carrying an imprecise modern catalogue title that omits the 1585 core. Recorded as probable rather than certain: the catalogue gives no leaf count and the volume is undigitised, so the one remaining confirmation — does GKS 1829 contain the 1585 observations / have 214 leaves — needs the digitised image or on-site inspection.

questions.title: Was the Apologia ad Craigum ever printed (Uraniburgi 1591)?
questions.hypothesis: Bartholin claimed to own a printed copy (De cometis 1665); Lalande & Houzeau–Lancaster list a print 'Uraniburgi 1591, 4°'; Friis & Dreyer conclude it was never printed and trace the 1591 entry to Lalande/Delambre.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31, high confidence NOT printed): the three authorities on Tycho's press — Friis, Dreyer and Nielsen (Bogtrykkeri 1921, pp.194–95) — agree no print was ever issued; the 'Uraniburgi 1591' imprint is a bibliographic ghost originating with Lalande (Bibliographie astronomique 1803) and repeated by Delambre and Houzeau–Lancaster. Tycho had meant to append the Apologia to De mundi Book II (letter to Hagecius, 25 Jan 1590) but dropped the plan; it circulated only as scribal copies. The lone contrary datum is Erasmus Bartholin's first-person 1665 ownership claim, which no located copy supports — but it is not dismissible (the Berlin fragment seems copied from a print), so this remains a genuine residual doubt rather than a refuted claim. Closing it fully would need a located printed copy or a pre-Bartholin independent reference.

questions.title: Map all manuscript witnesses (afskrifter) of the Apologia across libraries
questions.hypothesis: Nielsen notes 'flere Afskrifter'; KB NKS 93b is one; a fragment exists in Berlin (apparently copied from the supposed print, prefaced by Craig's three letters); Gassendi names a Longomontanus copy later held by Jørgen From.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): witness census assembled. CONFIRMED located — (1) KB NKS 2° 93 b, 40 ll., 32×21 cm, the scribal base-MS for Dreyer's TBOO IV edition; (2) Berlin, a fragment in a Brahe collection-volume, copied from a print and prefaced by Craig's three letters — exact shelfmark unresolved, its post-WWII Berlin-vs-Kraków fate unverified (see Q_APOLOGIA_RESIDUAL). REPORTED but untraced — (3) a Kepler-papers copy titled 'Apologia … ad Craigum de Cometis 1589'; (4) the Longomontanus→Jørgen From manuscript (Gassendi). Nielsen's 'flere Afskrifter' implies at least one further KB copy. Residual: pin the Berlin shelfmark and trace the Kepler/From copies.

questions.title: NKS 296 — confirm Tycho authorship and which nativity
questions.hypothesis: KB lists Tycho as creator; the German Urtheil likely accompanies one of the royal horoscopes (Christian IV / Ulrik / Hans).
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31, via the KB Primo record): NKS 296 is a German-language copy of the astrological Urtheil on the nativity of the young Prince CHRISTIAN (future Christian IV), cast 1577 by order of Frederik II. The catalogue subjects are Frederik II + Christian IV, and it explicitly cross-refers GKS 1820/1821, Thott 831/1611 and NKS 620 c — the documented Christian IV horoscope cluster. The Urtheil text is Tycho's; the physical NKS 296 is a LATER scribal copy (dated 16??–17??), not a Tycho autograph. A hand image is no longer needed to identify it.

questions.title: GKS 320 Astronomia hypothetica — Tycho's hand or an assistant's?
questions.hypothesis: A four-world-systems treatise catalogued in the Tycho orbit; the hand and authorship were unverified, with Tycho vs an assistant the assumed options.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31, via the KB Primo record): neither — it is the autograph of GEORG LUDWIG FROBENIUS (1566–1645), mathematician and bookseller. The full title compares the systems 'secundum Ptolomæum, Copernicum, Tychonem Braheum et Longomontanum … juxta Astronomiæ Danicæ placita' and is marked 'Mspt. autogr.'; comparing Tycho's system WITH Longomontanus's and citing the Astronomia Danica (1622) places it firmly after Tycho's death, so it cannot be his. Tycho is only one of the four hypotheses compared. GKS 320 is a 17th-c. reception/Nachleben object, re-attributed accordingly; no Brahe/Longomontanus hand comparison is warranted.

questions.title: Trace the lost 8vo observation volume 1563–74
questions.hypothesis: The 8vo autograph observations 1563–74 are on Bartholin's 1664 receipt; the volume later vanished. The earlier guess that it was lost in Paris during the La Hire loan turns out to be wrong.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31, confidence high): provenance chain reconstructed from three primary sources via Dreyer's Thesaurus Observationum edition. The 8vo was (1) on Bartholin's receipt of 20 June 1664; (2) seen in La Hire's room in Paris on 4 May 1697 (Rostgaard's letter of 10 May 1697); (3) RETURNED to Copenhagen with the rest in 1707 — so it was NOT lost during the La Hire loan; (4) borrowed (with the other volumes) by Christian Hvass in Feb 1778 and never returned; (5) last traced to a Hvass at Passy, near Paris, claiming to own 'an autograph of Tycho Brahe' (Neues Allg. Intelligenzblatt, Leipzig 1804). STILL LOST; last documented at Passy 1804. Its contents survive in KB GKS 1824 (Codex A) and GKS 310 (Bartholin's Collectio).

questions.title: Reconcile the Vienna apographa (19 fair-copy volumes) against KB originals
questions.hypothesis: Tycho's archive split: originals at KB, the neat yearly fair-copies at Vienna; the two halves needed cross-linking object by object.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-30): All 19 apographa (Cod. 10657–10675) are now enumerated with correct year/leaf data (ÖNB Tabulae codicum VI) and each is cross-linked to its KB autograph protocol via a `fair copy of` edge. See Q_APOGRAPHA_COLLATE for the year-by-year apparatus. Remaining work is digitisation/online access (Q_DIGITISE_VIENNA), not identification.

questions.title: Digitisation targets: undigitised autograph observation logs
questions.hypothesis: None of the 18 KB autograph observation volumes is digitised, yet they are the highest-value originals; a prioritised scan request was the deliverable.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31) — prioritised KB scan list, autograph-density first: (1) GKS 1822 (Horoscope of Prince Ulrik, wholly in Tycho's hand); (2) GKS 1825 / Codex B (mostly autograph, 1577–81, portrait+arms binding); (3) GKS 311 / Codex C (the 1582–86 anchor of the collation apparatus, partly autograph); (4) GKS 314 / Codex F (1595, many autograph entries, complete); (5) GKS 316–317 / Codices G–H (1596–99, incl. David Fabricius's autograph leaves + Kepler's declaration); (6) GKS 312–313, 318 / Codices D, E, I; (7) the quarto transcripts GKS 1824/1828 (incl. the unique 1593 transcript). Digitising tiers 1–3 first maximises autograph + apparatus value per krone. UPDATE 2026-06-07: GKS 316 folio (Codex G, 1596–97) and GKS 1824 kvart (earliest 1563–82) are now confirmed digitised on KB Digital Collections (object856355 and object77724 respectively). Remaining 16 KB protocols still undigitised.

questions.title: Locate copies of the lost occasional poems (Gjøe, Lange, Hans Frandsen)
questions.hypothesis: Tycho printed companion poems to Falk Gjøe and to Erik Lange (1584) and an elegy on Hans Frandsen; all lost as printed broadsheets, known only from letters/reprints.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): no printed broadsheet of any of the three survives (none in Bibliotheca Danica, USTC, KB, or any census; none carries a Nielsen Dansk-Bibliografi number). Their TEXTS, however, fare differently: the Erik Lange poem — Tycho's own diary calls it the FIRST thing ever printed on the Uraniborg press, 27 Nov 1584 — survives via Dreyer's Opera Omnia (and tekstnet/renæssancesprog); the Hans Frandsen elegy (Frandsen d. 4 July 1584) survives via Gassendi 1654/55 (pp.261–62) and Resen 1668 (pp.83–84); the Falk Gjøe poem is essentially text-lost, known only from Rothmann's 1587 letter about its emblematic vignettes (later reused on the press) and Tycho's reply (Epist. astron. p.89). A residual long-shot: a Gjøe/Lange broadsheet surfacing undetected in a Scandinavian collection.

questions.title: Find physical copies of the reissues KB holds only digitally
questions.hypothesis: KB holds the 1602 Nuremberg Mechanica and the 1603 Prague De mundi only as digital reproductions (re-verified 2026-05-31: both are 'Online resource' records at soeg.kb.dk, no physical shelfmark).
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): physical copies located and two best candidates linked as objects. Mechanica 1602 (VD17 23:270097W; Norman 320) survives widely — ETH Zürich (Rar 1371, e-rara, now linked), SLUB Dresden (Astron.82-1,misc.1; Astron.83), Smithsonian Dibner (q QB85.B7 1602), Glasgow (Sp Coll Ea8-x.15), Carnegie Mellon Posner (P77), RAS London, Library of Congress, Harry Ransom Center, Linda Hall. De mundi 1603 (Prague/Schumann) — Library of Congress (QB41 .B735 1603, now linked), Stanford (QB41 .B72 1603), ETH (e-rara 358757), Linda Hall; caveat: the 1603 is mostly 1588 sheets + new Prague prelims, so OPACs often record it under 1588 and the two states need care to distinguish.

questions.title: Track the De Gheyn portrait states across editions
questions.hypothesis: The De Gheyn copper-portrait of Tycho appears across the Epistolae / Mechanica / Progymnasmata in differing forms; the scholarship needed to be pinned down.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31, confidence high): per the New Hollstein catalogue raisonné (De Gheyn Family, 2000) — corroborated by Mortensen 1946, Van Regteren Altena 1983, Christianson 2000, Huizinga 1910 — these are TWO separate copperplates, not states of one. Portrait A (bare-headed, NH 238) exists in two states (I without address; II adding 'Marco Sadeler excudit'), carries heraldic errors (Hønnor/Belker), is the rarer plate, supplied the model for Tycho's oval supralibros ex-libris stamp, and was used posthumously in SOME copies of the 1602 Progymnasmata (printed on the title verso). Portrait B (plumed beret, NH 239, corrected heraldry; existed by Dec 1590 per Tycho's letter sending engraved copies) is the one pasted on the title verso in most copies of the 1596 Epistolae and the 1598 Mechanica — some Mechanica copies instead carry a watercolour portrait, and the Kiel Fabricius copy none. The 1602 Hülsius Mechanica title portrait is NOT a De Gheyn: it is an anonymous SAME-DIRECTION copy of Portrait B (corrected 2026-06-03 — New Hollstein records the NH239 copies as 'in same direction'; the 'mirrored' label was Huizinga's, from comparing the beret-portrait to the bare-headed Portrait A, NH238). Hülsius's 1601 Nuremberg Epistolarum reissue carries a SEPARATE, distinct same-direction copy of Portrait B on the title verso — so Nuremberg copying of the portrait for Hülsius began in 1601, a year before the Mechanica (see Q_MECH1602_ENGRAVER). Residual: copy-by-copy state assignment within the 1598 Mechanica and 1602 Progymnasmata still needs in-hand comparison (the Mechanica census has begun this).

questions.title: Reconstruct Tycho's own library (Bibliotheca Tychoniana) via /bibliotheca
questions.hypothesis: Tycho's working library — the books he OWNED and read, distinct from the works he created (this thesaurus's spine) — was largely dispersed; a core (~110 vols) reached the Prague Clementinum and was studied by Kleinschnitzová (1933) and Šolc (2002). It had not been reconstructed as a structured whole — until now.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): built as the library reconstruction 'tycho-brahe-library' — the Bibliotheca pillar of this portal, whose dashboard carries the current totals (attested entries, located works and volumes, still-missing titles). No snapshot counts are quoted here: the reconstruction moves as missing titles are located, and the dashboard's federation card always shows the live figures. Keyed on Tycho's ownership marks (gilt supralibros portrait-and-arms binding, 'T.B.O.' / 'T.B.O. 1576' stamps, autograph inscriptions). Five dispersal channels modelled — Clementinum/Jesuit core (~110 vols, 'Ex bibliotheca Tychoniana' 1642), heirs' sale, 1648 Swedish war-loot, Rudolfine-imperial absorption, attrition. Now federated into this thesaurus: a dashboard card reads its live counts, and the located and digitised Clementinum survivors are harvested here as owned-book objects, each linking back to its library entry — the sibling reconstruction to the works-spine and the Mechanica census. Residual: the remaining ghost entries to locate, and dispersal-channel assignment for the unassigned entries.

questions.title: When and how was the 1593 Vienna fair-copy lost?
questions.hypothesis: The 1593 apographum is the one gap in the Cod. 10657–10675 run, so the Historia Coelestis (printed from Vienna) lacks 1593 while it survives KB-only (Codex K / GKS 1828). The moment of loss is unfixed: before Tengnagel's 1604 handover to Kepler, between then and the 1621 imperial reclamation, or in Curtz's custody.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-06-01, to the limit of the documentary record): the terminus ante quem is Kepler's death, 15 November 1630. The prolegomena to the observation volumes of Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia (Dreyer, TBOO X) state the 1593 fair-copy 'had already been completely lost before Kepler's death'; the Copenhagen Meddelelser (2006) commentary restates this and adds that whether the Vienna apographa reached Curtz via Kepler's 1621 surrender or via his son-in-law Jakob Bartsch's widow (Susanna Kepler) c.1634 is unknown. The archive entered Kepler's custody through the 1604 Tengnagel–Kepler contract (recited in Ferdinand II's 1621 letter), so the loss falls in 1604×1630 and cannot be narrowed further, nor the mechanism fixed. The 'sent to Cassel and there lost' story Albert Curtz (Lucius Barrettus) put in the Historia Coelestis (1666) prolegomena is a fabrication papering over a gap that already existed when he received the nineteen volumes — Dreyer (Tycho Brahe, 1890, Appendix; and TBOO) debunks it. 1593 survives KB-only: Codex K (GKS 1828 Fasc. I, ending Venus 25 Sep 1593) + four appended leaves in Codex E (GKS 313). Residual: only a 1604–1630 inventory — Kepler's note on the Codex G front board (GKS 316), or Curtz's memorandum to Count Martinitz printed in Kästner, Geschichte der Mathematik II (1797) p.651ff — could fix whether 1593 was already gone at the 1604 handover.

questions.title: Census the surviving Icones instrumentorum broadsheets (LN 975/976)
questions.hypothesis: The Icones (engraved instrument plates, Uraniborg c.1596; LN 975 in 4°, LN 976 in 2°) are 'not at KB' — known copies are scattered (Wrocław, Stockholm, Vienna, Marburg) and have never been censused copy-by-copy.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): both Icones works are now censused copy-by-copy, and every scattered copy named here is enumerated. LN 975 → census brahe-icones-1596 (4 located copies: Wrocław/Breslau UB, Stockholm KB, Vienna ÖNB, and a fourth in private hands), with the two issue-states tracked — the standard Uraniborg setting (MS afterword on leaf 11, as in the Breslau copy) and the reset 'Wien' state (printed afterword, struck off-Hven c. early 1598, most likely Hamburg/de Ohr). LN 976 → census brahe-icones-duorum-1585 (Marburg, Hessisches Staatsarchiv — the sole known copy). 'Not at KB' confirmed: no Copenhagen copy surfaced in an Early European Books / ProQuest sweep of the KB holdings (31 May 2026). Residual: per-copy state and plate collation is begun but not yet exhaustive; the De Gheyn-portrait link is tracked at Q_DEGHEYN_STATES / Q_MECH1602_ENGRAVER.

questions.title: GKS 320 (Frobenius four-systems treatise) — provenance + is it otherwise known?
questions.hypothesis: Now re-attributed to Georg Ludwig Frobenius (Hamburg mathematician/bookseller, 1566–1645): a 17th-c. autograph comparing Ptolemy, Copernicus, Tycho and Longomontanus, drawing on the Astronomia Danica (1622). How a Hamburg autograph reached the Danish Royal Library, and whether the treatise survives in other copies or print, is unknown.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-06-01): both sub-questions answered. Georg Ludwig Frobenius (Iphofen 1566 – Hamburg 1645) was a Hamburg printer-bookseller who spent ~6 weeks in Tycho's familia on Hven in 1591 and in 1627 printed Longomontanus's Cyclometria (Christianson, On Tycho's Island pp.285–86) — not of the Basel Froben dynasty though he believed he was; GKS 320 draws on Longomontanus's Astronomia Danica (1622) so it is a Hamburg-period work. ACQUISITION (Brøndsted, Fund og Forskning 9, 1962, p.77 + n.10): GKS 320 is one of a 3-volume set of Frobenius printer's-manuscripts (Druckmanuskripte for books he never issued) — GKS 320–322 2°, the 'Astronomia hypothetica quadriformis' (this four-systems treatise) + an 'Astrologia Ovidiana'. On Frobenius's death at Hamburg in 1645 his literary remains passed to the Hamburg cathedral chapter (Domkapitel); when the Dombibliothek was dissolved and auctioned in the 18th c., the Royal Library Copenhagen bought them 'perhaps with a view to their Tycho-Brahe material' — exactly fitting the KB catalogue's 'Indlemmet i KB senest 1787'. So the route is Frobenius → Hamburg Dombibliothek → 18th-c. dissolution auction → KB, NOT the Gottorp channel earlier hypothesised. OTHERWISE-KNOWN: no printed version and no sibling MS (EEB/VD17/USTC negative) — a unique abandoned-publication manuscript. Residual: only the exact pre-1787 auction/accession entry would date the KB purchase precisely (archival nicety). A by-product of the same article: a previously unrecorded 1584 Tycho elegy on Ptolemy, surviving in Frobenius's 1644 Almagest proof-sheet at the Royal Library, Stockholm (object O_STOCKHOLM_FROBENIUS_CARMEN).

questions.title: GKS 1832 'Planetary tables' — is it in Erasmus Bartholin's hand?
questions.hypothesis: KB tentatively attributes the Tychonic-Keplerian planetary tables in GKS 1832 to Erasmus Bartholin, whose hand is well attested in the adjacent editorial volumes (GKS 308–310), so this is testable.
questions.resolves: OPEN (position as of 2026-06-02): the attribution is the Royal Library's own hedge, and the test that would settle it is one image short. The KB catalogue titles the volume 'Tabulæ Planetarum ex observationibus Tychonico-Keplerianis forte Er. Bartholini' — '…perhaps of Erasmus Bartholin' — and no published study of the hand exists. The volume's profile argues for caution: it is a quarto of Tychonic-Keplerian planetary tables, a working document of the 1660s rather than a primary observation log; it is absent from Picard's 1672 receipt of the five folio volumes taken to Paris; and it entered KB only by 1787 — a profile matching the later, separately-acquired Tychonica (cf. GKS 320, Q_GKS320_PROVENANCE) rather than the documented route of the Bartholin editorial archive. On that evidence a hand from Bartholin's circle (a student, or the young Ole Rømer) or a later Danish computational copy is at least as consistent with the record as Bartholin's own hand. A secure comparison basis exists: three signed Erasmus Bartholin Latin autographs of 1672–75 are digitised among the Royal Society's Early Letters — a fluent, lightly right-sloped humanist italic; one of the letters itself discusses Tycho's Hven observations, Picard, and the edition 'ex mea recensione', the very corpus GKS 1832 derives from. Bartholin's securely-attributed Copenhagen volumes (GKS 308–310) remain undigitised, as does GKS 1832 itself. What would settle it: a digitised image of GKS 1832, compared against the Royal Society autographs — ideally three-way, with a Rømer autograph as the principal alternative hand.

questions.title: Identify the engraver of the 1602 Mechanica title-portrait
questions.hypothesis: The 1602 Nuremberg/Hülsius Mechanica carries a printed engraved title-portrait that is an anonymous, SAME-DIRECTION (not mirror-reversed) copy after De Gheyn's hat-portrait (New Hollstein 239) — cut by a Nuremberg workshop hand in Hülsius's circle. (Tier A, 2026-06-22: derived from Hülsius's own 1601 Epistolarum plate; printed by Christoph Lochner.)
questions.resolves: OPEN (position as of 2026-06-22): everything except the engraver's personal name is settled. The 1602 title-portrait is an unsigned, same-direction copy after De Gheyn's beret-portrait of Tycho (New Hollstein 239; the genealogy runs Gemperlin's 1586 painting → De Gheyn's engraving, existing by December 1590 → the Nuremberg copies). It was cut from — or shares an exemplar with — the smaller plate Hülsius had already used in his 1601 Nuremberg Epistolarum reissue: both captions carry the same idiosyncratic engraver's errors (INSTVMENTORVM, ASTONOMICORVM, INVETORIS), which fixes the derivation, and both books were printed by Christoph Lochner for Levinus Hulsius. Neither Hülsius plate is recorded in the De Gheyn New Hollstein copy-list, and no signature or attribution exists in any catalogue, auction record or portrait index (VD17; the Digitaler Portraitindex, which records the plate 'nach Jaques de Gheyn … Unbez.' [unsigned]; Hollstein LX). The documentary evidence converges on the workshop of Johann Sibmacher — the only documented Hülsius engraver in Nuremberg, cutting plates for the same press in the same years and signing a comparable nobleman portrait engraving one year later (Adolf von Schwarzenberg, 1603) — but the Brahe plate's quality sits below Sibmacher's signed prime work, and Hollstein LX (Seelig 2002) does not list it, so the evidence cannot separate Sibmacher's own quick trade-plate from a hand in his large workshop. The most defensible attribution: an anonymous copperplate cut in the Sibmacher workshop (Hülsius's Nuremberg house engraving operation, Lochner's press), c.1601–02, after De Gheyn NH 239. What would settle it: expert adjudication by a print room — a connoisseurship comparison of the Brahe plate against the signed 1603 Schwarzenberg engraving and the 1602 Epitome Emblematum plates; an enquiry to the Germanisches Nationalmuseum's Graphische Sammlung is prepared.

questions.title: Locate + collate the Triangulorum praxis autograph leaves at Prague
questions.hypothesis: Autograph leaves of Tycho's trigonometry (Triangulorum planorum et sphæricorum praxis) survive at Prague, known from Studnička's 1886 facsimile, but the current shelfmark is unconfirmed and they have not been collated against the printed/edited text.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-06-01): shelfmark confirmed and the hand question settled. The MS is Prague, National Library of the Czech Republic (NKP, formerly the University Library), shelfmark NK 14 C 20 (old marks Truhlář nr 2761 / Kl. nr 12:2) — 'Triangulorum planorum [et sphæricorum] praxis arithmetica', 1591, in its original binding as the closing item of a trigonometry Sammelband opened by Rheticus's Canon doctrinae triangulorum (Norlind 1970 p.234; 'Tycho Brahe and Prague — Crossroads of European Science'). Two editions already exist — Studnička's 1886 Prague phototype facsimile and Dreyer's critical text TBOO I, 283–293 (set from this very MS) — so the 'collate against the edited text' action is effectively met by Dreyer's edition; there is no independent printing to collate against (the work was never printed in Tycho's lifetime). HAND: settled — the content is Tycho's, but the script is NOT his autograph. Dreyer (TBOO I, 315) already doubted Studnička's autograph attribution, and Šíma & Valeška's forensic paleography ('Analysis of Tycho's Handwritings', in Tycho Brahe and Prague, 2002, pp.150–167) is decisive: 'Not one of the manuscripts held by the National Library, Prague was written by Tycho's hand' — NK 14 C 20 is by a professional calligrapher (a different writer from NK XII A 28). Studnička's 1901 Tycho-autograph claim is thereby overturned. Residual: only a leaf-by-leaf image check of NK 14 C 20 against Dreyer's transcription (what the facsimile / TBOO each normalise), which needs the digitised or in-hand MS — a text-collation nicety, not an attribution question.

questions.title: Extract the Hven visitor register from the Notae historicae (Cod. 10718)
questions.hypothesis: Cod. 10718 (digitised) bundles the meteorological diary with the Notae historicae — Tycho's running note of who visited Uraniborg: a first-rate prosopographical source for the Hven network, never indexed as structured data.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-06-07). Location confirmed: ÖNB Vienna, Cod. Vindob. lat. 10718, digitised (viewer: https://viewer.onb.ac.at/131EA75D — catalogue: https://search.onb.ac.at/permalink/f/sb7jht/ONB_alma21303501260003338). The visitor register has been built from the 1876 print edition (Tyge Brahes meteorologiske Dagbog, Copenhagen) checked against TBOO IX, and is published as the structured layer of this portal's Diarium view: 250 entries (197 arrivals, 40 departures, 8 events, 4 deaths, 1 movement), 81% at confidence A, covering 4 Jun 1585 – 20 Apr 1597. Royal visitors: James VI of Scotland (20 Mar 1590), Queen Sophie (27–29 Jun 1586), Henry Julius of Brunswick (4 May 1590), Christian IV (3 Jul 1592), Duke Wilhelm of Courland (24 Aug 1592). Scholars: Rothmann (Aug–Sep 1590), Blaeu (winter 1595–96), Liddel (24 Jun 1587), Longomontanus (Oct 1595). Codicological: 191 leaves, quarto/oblong, parchment binding; written by assistants (primarily Elias Olsen Morsing until his death 11 Mar 1590); some leaves on Hven paper-mill stock (VRANIBVRGVM watermark).

questions.title: Relationship among the three ÖNB 1000-star restitution copies (Cod. 10705/06/07)
questions.hypothesis: ÖNB holds three copies of Tycho's 1600 restitution of the 1000-star catalogue (Cod. 10705 26 ll., 10706 26 ll., 10707 31 ll.); which is the master and how the three relate (copying order, added stars) is undetermined.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-06-01): the three are not a master-and-derivatives stemma but parallel PRESENTATION apographs of the 1004-star restitution (Stellarum inerrantium accurata restitutio, Wandsbek 1598/1600), copied by assistants. Their recipients differ: Cod. 10705 → Archduke Matthias; Cod. 10707 → Imperial Vice-Chancellor Rudolf Corraduz, dated by Tycho's autograph inscription March 1600 (Dreyer, TBOO III, 1916, p.417); Cod. 10706's recipient is unrecorded in both Dreyer's manuscript list (p.411) and Truffa's 2002 census. The 31-vs-26-leaf outlier 10707 is explained: it UNIQUELY carries the Stellarum inerrantium Restitutionis Appendix — 36 star-positions adapted to Rudolf II's nativity — which Dreyer printed for the first time from this codex alone (TBOO III, pp.379–389). No copying-order stemma was ever published: Dreyer judged collation of the apographs 'perfect waste of time' (Tycho Brahe, 1890, p.266) and based his edition on the Copenhagen copy GKS 306, not the Vienna ones; the modern machine-readable edition (Verbunt & van Gent, A&A 516, 2010, A28) followed him. RESIDUAL (reading-room only): the 10706 recipient + any leaf-level collation of the three against each other. (Distinct: Cod. 10709 is the earlier 1589 zodiacal catalogue, Dreyer's V¹, not a restitution copy.)

questions.title: Trace the untraced Apologia witnesses + resolve Berlin-vs-Kraków
questions.hypothesis: The Apologia witness census left two reported-but-untraced copies — a Kepler-papers copy ('Apologia … ad Craigum de Cometis 1589') and the Longomontanus→Jørgen From manuscript (Gassendi) — and the Berlin fragment's exact shelfmark is unresolved, with the ex-Preußische holdings split post-WWII between Berlin and the Jagiellońska, Kraków.
questions.resolves: OPEN (position as of 2026-06-02): the three threads now stand as follows. (1) The Longomontanus→Jørgen From copy — written at Tycho's dictation c.1589–90, passed from Longomontanus to Chancellor Christen Friis to Jørgen From, who quoted it at length in his 1642 Dissertatio astronomica and promised to print it — is untraced after From's death on 19 Aug 1651. The chain is anchored in primary sources: From's own Dissertatio; Ole Worm's letter to Gassendi of June 1648 (Gassendi, Opera Omnia 1658, p.518); Gassendi's Vita 1654, p.206; with Norlind 1970, pp.140–42, and Kragh, RePoSS #22, 2014, pp.37–40. (2) The Kepler-papers copy is real, distinct, and located: Norlind 1970 (pp.136–43) identifies it as Pulk. MSS Bd 19, fols. 115–150, Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences, St Petersburg — 36 leaves, lacking the first and last, read and corrected throughout by Tycho himself; it entered the Kepler Nachlass because Kepler was drafting his own, never-finished Craig rebuttal, and pre-war photostats survive at the Munich Kepler-Kommission. It is the mutilated, then-anonymous tract Hevelius described to Bullialdus (Hamburgische vermischte Bibliothek 2, 1744). (3) Berlin vs Kraków is settled: the Jagiellońska's two Brahe Sammelbände (BJ St. Dr. Cim. 6166–6167, the 1588 Hven edition, acquired by Jan Brożek in 1610; and Cim. 6169–6171, the 1603 Prague edition) are old Jagiellonian holdings that do not bind in the Apologia or Craig's letters, so the Berlin fragment is not at Kraków and is most likely a genuine WWII loss from the Preußische Staatsbibliothek — Norlind (p.138) already recorded it as lost. What remains: Martha List's 1961 inventory of the Kepler Nachlass for the modern St Petersburg shelfmark; the specific Berlin destruction or displacement event; and the From manuscript itself.

questions.title: Fold Bartholin's Specimen recognitionis (1668) into the spot-collation register
questions.hypothesis: Bartholin's Specimen recognitionis (1668) is 36 pp. of published 1582 collation — Curtz's printed readings set against Tycho's autograph — i.e. a ready-made, citable variant set the new 1582 variant register (Q_SPOTCOLLATE) did not yet incorporate.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-06-01, first tranche folded in; full transcription mechanical): the Specimen is located and incorporated into the 1582 variant register. The 1668 print is fully digitised (archive.org, from the Google Books scan of the Naples copy, public domain). Its 31-page errata table for 1582 is keyed to the 1666 Historia Coelestis pagination in the form 'Pag. n. colum. n. lin. n. pro [printed] leg. [corrected]', and its introduction enumerates six error classes (omitted day-definitions, gross digit errors, transposed zodiac/planet symbols, wrong times, neglected/confused observations, mis-ordered observations). A representative sample of the variants — marked provisional until checked against the page images — is in the register with the access reference. This gives 1582 a published, citable variant set independent of the Opera Omnia harvest — exactly the gap the question named. Residual (mechanical, same ceiling as the rest of the register): a clean image-based transcription of all ~300–450 entries, since the scan's automated text garbles the Latin and its numeric and symbol readings are unreliable.

questions.title: Which apographa are in Longomontanus's hand vs other assistants?
questions.hypothesis: The 19 fair-copies are attributed wholesale to Longomontanus, but the copying spanned 1582–1601 and the familia rotated; Dreyer notes Tycho's own hand appears often in the earlier volumes and rarely in the later, implying multiple scribes.
questions.resolves: OPEN (position as of 2026-06-22): the wholesale attribution of the 19 Vienna fair-copies to Longomontanus is an inference, not a documented fact, and it has been replaced by a per-volume, graded attribution. Dreyer's only direct statement (TBOO X prolegomena, p.XVIII) is an aggregate gradient — 'In prioribus tomis satis multa inveniuntur Tychonis manu scripta, in posterioribus pauca' (Tycho's own hand frequent in the earlier volumes, rare in the later) — and he names no scribe; no published source gives a per-volume hand attribution. Overlaying the familia's documented service dates on each volume's observation year (contemporaneous copying — a model Dreyer's gradient itself supports, since a single retrospective copyist would have left a uniform hand and no gradient) yields the graded candidate set now shown on each observation volume: the seven 1582–88 volumes (Cod. 10657–10663) exclude Longomontanus, who reached Hven only in summer 1589/90, and belong to the early familia (Flemløse, Sascerides, Morsing, Hans Crol) with Tycho's own frequent hand; 1590–95 (Cod. 10665–10669, less the lost 1593) have Longomontanus as the strongly-favoured hand, 1592 and 1594 the cleanest (sole senior assistant); 1589, 1596–97 and 1600–01 are genuine splits (Morsing/Flemløse/Crol at the 1589 turnover; Johannes Eriksen 1596–97; Longomontanus returned, Eriksen and Tengnagel at Prague 1600–01); and 1598–99 (Cod. 10672–10673) are unattributed exile volumes. Confirmation needs a securely-attributed Longomontanus autograph as comparand. Two are now identified, neither digitised: his letter to Kepler in Vienna (Cod. lat. 10703, f.236v) and his album-amicorum leaf of 13 September 1598, signed at Wandsbek the same day as Tycho's own, among the Boetius album leaves of the Noodt collection at the Royal Library, Copenhagen (Thott 500,2° / Thott 1059,2°; Helk, Fund og Forskning 21, 1974). What would settle it: an image of either autograph, compared first against the strongly-favoured volumes (Cod. 10665–10669), then a volume-by-volume examination of the whole series.

questions.title: Expand the Vienna convolutes (Cod. 10686/10688/10689) to per-part records
questions.hypothesis: Three Sammelbände hold many individual Tycho items between them (letters, treatises, Kepler editorial notes, polemics), catalogued at part level but once summarised as one row each.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31): the per-part expansion is in the graph — 89 sub-part records (Cod. 10686 ×48, Cod. 10688 ×13, Cod. 10689 ×28) are recorded as child objects under their parent convolute, each with genre, authorship-direction and notes; 78 of 89 carry an ÖNB AC permalink and 11 are digitised with viewer URLs. Residual is minor: ~11 leaf-range parts (e.g. /71–78) still lack an isolated AC number — a clean-up, not a discovery question.

questions.title: Digitisation: almost none of the Vienna Tycho codices are online
questions.hypothesis: Only 13 of 127 ÖNB Tycho objects are digitised (incl. Cod. 10718 and Cod. 10688/17); the 19 apographa and most treatises are not. A prioritised request was the deliverable.
questions.resolves: RESOLVED (2026-05-31) — prioritised ÖNB digitisation list: (1) the 19 yearly apographa Cod. 10657–10675 in full — the half of the split observation archive that is the citation-text behind the Historia Coelestis, and the partner side of the new KB↔Vienna apparatus (collation by image becomes possible once these are online); within them, lead with 1599/Cod. 10673 (the corrected volume) and the years flagged in the discrepancy register (1584, 1589–91); (2) the star-catalogue restitutions Cod. 10705–10707 + the right-ascension catalogue 10709; (3) the treatise codices 10721 (De nova stella materials), 10558 (trigonometry); (4) the three convolutes 10686/10688/10689 part by part. The apographa series is the unambiguous first ask.

questions.title: Did Tycho Brahe or Jon Jacobsen Venusin write Urania Titani?
questions.hypothesis: Zeeberg (1994) established Tycho's authorship via the Craig letter (26 July 1594, TBOO VII.366): 'lusus … in honorem sororis nomine a me compositus' — a composition written 'in his sister's name', the epistolary fiction of the poem. Against this, Andersen-Vinilandicus (in Kunstværket og dets hemmeligheder, 2009, pp. 225–276) proposes Jon Jacobsen Venusin (d. 1608), Gellius Sascerides's brother-in-law: a Hermetically-oriented neo-Latin poet with documented Hven visits (20–22 May 1590; 29 Nov–3 Dec 1595) who could have been a ghost-author for the poem. Venusin is not Gellius Sascerides — they are distinct persons.
questions.resolves: OPEN (position as of 2026-06-13): Tycho's authorship stands but is dented. The Craig letter identifies a composition 'written in Sophie's name' without naming the poem explicitly, so the identification is probabilistic; and Zeeberg's arguments were framed to defeat the Sophie-as-author hypothesis (Resen 1668; DBL3 1979), not to anticipate a Venusin candidacy. Venusin's two documented Hven visits (May 1590; Nov–Dec 1595) do not coincide with the winter 1594 composition date, which weakens but does not eliminate his case. The key primary evidence is the correction stratigraphy of Cod. Vindob. 10686/12: Tycho's autograph corrections (hand T) against the remaining corrections by a second hand. Path to resolution: read Andersen-Vinilandicus 2009 in full, and compare the second hand in the Vienna manuscript against Venusin's autographs as catalogued by Andersen, 'Venusins Autografer', Fund og Forskning 60 (2022), pp. 49ff.

movements.label: Reclaimed for the Emperor → Imperial Library

discriminators.confounder: Erik Lange (1553-1613), alchemist, Tycho's brother-in-law (m. Sophie Brahe)
discriminators.why: Independent humanist cursive of broadly the same school; co-located in the same album (Sebald Plan, Pillar 2) and circulated through the Brahe-Lange orbit (Sophie Brahe's Eriksholm library).
First lead assistant (1577-88); observation-log entries; later Bishop of Bergen.
Hven assistant 1585-92; carried De mundi to Kassel and Tübingen in 1588 (so his hand may appear on De mundi-orbit documents).
The most prolific Tycho-circle copyist (1589-97, returned 1600-01); engrossed most letters and observations. The default author of 'Hven-period Latin' that gets loosely called Tycho's.
Friis (1876) determined by HANDWRITING ANALYSIS that Morsing kept the meteorological diary on Hven for most of 13 Apr 1583 - 5 Apr 1589 — so the 'Tycho's weather diary' is largely Morsing's hand.

discriminators.confounder: Otto Brahe (Otte Axelsen Brahe, 1579-1611), Tycho's nephew
discriminators.why: Same family/school; album entry co-located in VI F 44 alongside Tycho's.
Visited Hven briefly in 1580; his heavily-annotated De revolutionibus (Prague NK 14 B 16) was for over a century described as Tycho's annotated copy. The canonical Tycho misattribution.
misattributions: De revolutionibus marginalia (Prague NK 14 B 16, Basel 1566): reattributed from Tycho to Paul Wittich by Gingerich & Westman 1981 (JHA 12:53–54; full case in the Annotated Census 2002), independently corroborated by Edward Rosen, 'Don't Give Tychon What Isn't Brahe's', Kwartalnik HNiT 26/3-4 (1981) 549–564, and by Šíma–Valeška 2002. THE canonical debunked Tycho-hand claim — in the Debunked Claims Register.

discriminators.confounder: Professional calligrapher(s) of the presentation copies (≥2 distinct hands)
discriminators.why: Tycho used professional calligraphers to PAINT the bodies of presentation dedications (Mechanica Pillars 3-5; the Tabulae Sinuum; the two Prague trig pamphlets). The body is calligraphic; only the signature is autograph — but the whole leaf gets called 'Tycho's hand'.
misattributions: Triangulorum planorum praxis arithmetica (NK 14 C 20, 1591): Studnička 1901 published as Tycho holograph; Šíma-Valeška: 'undoubtedly the work of a professional calligrapher'. Mathematics is Tycho's; the scribe is not.
Brevissimum planimetriae compendium (NK XII A 28): Studnička 1903 published as Tycho; Šíma-Valeška: a professional writer, and a DIFFERENT one from NK 14 C 20.

discriminators.confounder: Frans Gansneb Tengnagel von Camp (1573-1636), pupil, son-in-law, posthumous editor
discriminators.why: Took custody of Tycho's instruments and observations after 1601 and edited portions of the Progymnasmata (Prague 1602); many subsequent documents ABOUT Tycho are in Tengnagel's hand and risk being read as Tycho's.

Tyge sometimes signed AS IF his father, leaving only a 'T(ychonis) F(ilius)' afterthought to distinguish them. A bare 'Tÿcho Brahe' signature could be father or son; he outlived his father by 26 years.
misattributions: Detmold Mechanica dedication (legacy 'Pillar 5b'): signed 'Tÿcho Brahe T.F.', correlates with Tyge's hand (VI F 44 verso), NOT the astronomer — Šíma-Valeška 'Nihil obstat'. A document signed as if by the father, actually by the son.
